reference.title: wear, carry, or dress?
reference.text: Use wear for clothes and jewellery / glasses, etc.: She’s wearing a hat. He’s wearing sunglasses. Use carry for bags, cases, etc.: I can’t carry this case. She’s carrying a bag. Use dress (with no object) to describe the kind of clothes people wear: The Italians dress very well. Lucy always dresses in black.

reference.title: a pair
reference.text: We often use a pair to talk about plural clothes, e.g. a pair of shoes, trainers, boots, jeans, trousers, etc.

reference.title: /ə/ and /ɜː/
reference.text: /ə/ is a short sound. It is only in unstressed syllables: computer, trousers, cardigan. /ɜː/ is a long sound. It is in stressed syllables and short words: shirt, first, work. The letters er, ir, ur, and or after w are often /ɜː/ when they are stressed: her, first, curly, work.

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You and the student ask and answer: What clothes do you usually wear… for work / university / school? when you go out at night? when you want to relax at the weekend? for a special occasion? reference.title: Present continuous: be + verb + -ing
rows: Yes, I am. / No, I’m not.
Yes, we are. / No, we aren’t.
Yes, he is. / No, he isn’t.

reference.title: Use
reference.text: We use the present continuous: 1 for things happening now, at this moment: A What are you doing? B I’m sending a message to Sarah. 2 for temporary things that are happening around now, this week, etc.: My brother is doing a two-month course in the UK. 3 to describe what’s happening in a picture: In this picture the woman is standing near a table.

reference.title: Spelling: -ing form
rows: cut the final e and add -ing
consonant-vowel-consonant: double the final consonant and add -ing

reference.title: Present simple or present continuous?
rows: present simple: things that are generally true or always happen
A What do you do? B I work for an IT company.
present continuous: an action happening now, at this moment
A What are you doing? B I’m checking my messages.
non-action verbs (want, need, like…) — present simple
I like this painting, it’s beautiful.

reference.why: like is a non-action verb (like want, need): we use it in the present simple, not the present continuous.

reference.title: The Remake Project
reference.text: The Remake Project was the idea of Canadian artist Jeff Hamada. He asked readers of his website to remake a famous work of art as a photo. Hundreds of people sent photos to the project and the photos appeared in blogs, in newspapers, and in a book.

reference.title: Describing a picture (a painting or photo)
reference.text: When we describe a picture, we normally use There is / There are to say what’s in the picture, and we use the present continuous to say what the people are doing, e.g. There’s a table with some bread on it. The woman is standing next to the table.
